Almost every sector in the city is plagued with the problem of stray dogs. While there was a proposal to construct a dog pound, no site has been earmarked for the purpose.

Mayor Pardeep Chhabra has, meanwhile, assured that suitable action would be taken soon.

Heading: Vigilance Awareness Week concludes in PGI - Indian Express
Content:
The decomposed bodies of an unidentified women, said to be in her 20s and a girl were found in a wide pit near Panchkula Information Technology (IT) park late on Friday evening.

The two had been reportedly strangulated to death before being burnt. Local labourers in the area noticed the bodies and informed the police.

"While the woman appears to be in her 20s, the girl was around three years old. The bodies were found from a secluded area and the two appeared to be migrants," said a police officer who did not wish to be identified.

Strands of the woman's hair and pieces of broken bangles were found near the spot, indicating the possibility of a struggle.

The bodies were later shifted to the mortuary at the General Hospital in Sector 6 and the police have registered a case.

Heading: Sector 18 residents want shops shifted from green belt - Indian Express
Content:
PGI Director K K Talwar presided over the closing function of the Vigilance Awareness Week on Friday and also distributed prizes to the winners. The Vigilance Week was observed in the hospital from November 3 to 7.

Professor Talwar stressed the need for complete dedication and devotion by the employees. Anil Kumar Gupta, deputy director (administration)-cum-chief vigilance officer, welcomed the chief guest and also spoke on the occasion.

Sandeep Kaur won the first prize while Amarjeet Kaur Nafra and B M Dhawan stood second and third respectively in the essay writing competition. In the slogan writing competition, Dr Inderpal Singh Sahni stood first while Jatinder Kumar stood second and Manju Dhawan stood third. In the quiz contest, Ajay Atri got the first prize (he also stood third in declamation contest) while Bharti Sharma and Avinash Verma came second and third respectively. In the declamation contest, the first position went to Varpreet Kaur while the second and third position was bagged by Ninjit and Chandanpreet.

Heading: Movie reviews - Indian Express
Content:
Advani's b'day BJP's lucky day?
A majority of senior Delhi BJP leaders are queuing up to file their nominations on Saturday — the birthday of their chief L K Advani who turns 81.
The BJP chief ministerial candidate V K Malhotra, leader of Opposition Jagdish Mukhi, Hari Nagar candidate Harsharan Balli, Nangloi candidate Raj Singh, Dwarka candidate Pradyuman Rajput, Brijwasan candidate Satyaprakash Rana and several others have decided to file their nominations tomorrow.
Many including Balli would first visit Advani's residence to seek his blessings before filing nominations.

Poonam's volte face
Poonam Azad's fall from grace is pitiable. After the aggressive campaigning during the last Assembly elections, she is stranded ticketless this year. Azad had a taste of her party's attitude towards her on Wednesday.
After her much-publicised resgination, when she reached the party president Rajnath Singh's residence to submit her resignation, neither Singh nor his secretary were present. The staff told Azad to drop her resignation in a drop box and leave. The very next day Azad did flip-flop and blushingly re-entered the party fold.

Heading: Construction of two Panchkula flyovers to be delayed - Indian Express
Content:
QUANTUM OF SOLACE

CAST: Daniel Craig, Judi Dench, Mathieu Amalric, Olga Kurylenko, Gemma Aterton

DIRECTOR: Marc Foster

This 007 had everything going for it: Daniel Craig, who wowed audiences and critics alike in his first outing as Bond, not a mean feat considering how long the hunt was for the new MI6 agent; Judi Dench in a meatier role as M; Paul Haggis (Crash, In the Valley of Elah) as writer; and Marc Foster (Monster's Ball, Finding Neverland) as director.

However, Quantum of Solace ain't no Casino Royale. That film gave us a Bond we had never seen before: a bruised and confused 007, as capable of getting hurt as hurting. He found and lost love in the film, going through a betrayal in the middle.

Though Quantum of Solace picks up from there, with a Bond determined to avenge that love, against unknown forces who killed her, it eventually turns out to be just an excuse to hang two hours of uninterrupted— interchangeable with convolute— action and some great actors on (including the two Bond women, with not a decent cocktail dress between them).

The plot, moving from Rome to London to Haiti to Austria to Bolivia, back to Italy, then to Russia, is so complicated that you better give up pretending you care. Greedy dictators, compromised governments and oil politics are thrown about.

It doesn't help that the villain apparently running circles around half the world's governments is an effete pretender (Almeric) who probably won't be able to convince a classroom of kids of his eco-friendly intentions. To dress him up in Hawaiian shirts and a languorous gait is an insult to our intelligence.

Craig looks great and, once in a while, still uses those piercing blue eyes to good effect. But he has none of the spark, wit or wisdom to transcend him above the other —B — Jason Bourne.

As boats crash into ships, planes collide into mountains and entire hotels go up in blasts, we are left looking for precisely the same thing as Bond apparently is: some quantum of solace. None of us is getting it, at least in this film. shalini.langer@expressindia.com

EMI

CAST: Sanjay Dutt, Arjun Rampal, Malaika Arora Khan, Urmila Matondkar, Ashish Choudhary

DIRECTOR: Saurabh Kabra

There are two films in—EMI — one, in which Malaika Arora Khan comes on every 10 minutes shaking her booty, in clothes getting skimpier by the minute, and another, in which four old men have a genuine conversation about their children in which the latter are allowed to have ambitions and to travel abroad without breaking their parents' hearts.

The sad part is that while Kabra could nicely shake and mix up the two, he makes no effort to. The two films run parallel in EMI, the good parts being interspersed with the truly appalling.

And Kabra is working with a nice idea here and a fairly good script involving four different families who have all taken loans and are now defaulting on their EMIs for varied reasons. One a newly married and quickly separated couple; another a DJ who spends more than he earns; the third a father who has borrowed to send his son abroad; and fourth a woman paying off the mob to get her husband's suicide turned into a murder to claim the Rs 2-crore insurance.

There are some very funny moments, like the smooth-talking personal bankers who won't be fazed by lecherous customers or cautious ones; the innovative gangsters who help you in getting bank loans so you can pay up their money, in installments; Sanjay Dutt, who can now do these roles of a kind-hearted gangster in his sleep and who here, in the placement of his expensive dark glasses a little too unevenly down his nose, conveys both his ambitions and limitations; and his gang of small, Munnabhai-esque lumpens.

And there are some very unfunny ones: Rampal, confusing himself once again as a serious musician (in a tweed hat, for God's sake); Choudhary's twitching moustache that has more emotion than the rest of his face combined; Urmila's grieving-widow act dressed in expensive saris, including a transparent red piece, designer suits and twirling wine; and Malaika's ever-shortening wardrobe.

Please, for our sake and yours, get a makeover.

shubhra.gupta@gmail.com

Heading: Kalka-Pinjore highway: HC pulls up NHAI, HVPNL - Indian Express
Content:
The construction of two major flyovers — one at Majri chowk in Old Panchkula and the other at Chandimandir — have been delayed as the land acquired for the project is different from what was shown in the masterplan, sources said.

The flyovers are part of the bigger project of the Zirakpur-Parwanoo four-laning project by the National Highway Authority of India (NHAI).

"The planned land that was to be given by the NHAI for the construction of the flyover at Majri chowk in Old Panchkula and the one in the army area for the Chandimandir flyover is different from the actual land that is being acquired by the NHAI for the same. Because of this, the designs had to be changed, which have now been sent for approval," said an official of the Jai Prakash Associates, the company handling the project.

He added that the army land, earmarked for the Chandimandir flyover, was handed over to them recently by the authorities. "Under the new design of the flyover, there would be a complete shift of the structure by a few metres affecting the complete patch from Majri chowk to Burj Kotia. While work for the various underpasses has started, work on the Chandimandir flyover will start by December-end and on Majri Chowk flyover by January next year," said the official.

Structures under the project

* Zirakpur- Parwanoo four-laning

* Six-lane rail overbridge (Zirakpur)

* Underpass near Sector 20

* Subway near Sector 20

* Underpass near Sector 21 (opposite Tau Devi Lal Stadium)

* Underpass near Sector 2

* Six-lane flyover at Majri Chowk

* Subway on the highway near DC office

* Six-lane flyover at Chandimandir

* Underpass near Saket Hospital

* Bridge parallel to existing bridge on Jhajra river

* Pinjore-Parwanoo bypass

Heading: Guru Nanak College edge out PU Campus - Indian Express
Content:
Making it clear that all kinds of hindrances and roadblocks on the Pinjore-Kalka highway should be cleared with immediate effect, the Punjab and Haryana High Court took the National Highway Authority of India (NHAI) to task on Friday.

The conduct and lackadaisical attitude of NHAI came under the scanner of a division bench comprising Justice Uma Nath Singh and Justice Daya Chaudhary. "Despite stern attitude, you are taking it lightly. If there is any delay, you will suffer. There is no dearth of funds but there seems to be dearth of will. If you don't complete work, we will exclude you from working and hand over the case to the Central government. You seem to have confusion about our powers," observed Justice Uma Nath Singh. The Court also took the Haryana Vidyut Parisaran Nigam Limited (HVPNL) to task for not showing interest in removing roadblocks on the Kalka-Pinjore Highway. Advocate Amit Jhanji, counsel appearing for Himalayan Express (concessionaire) apprised the court that the concessionaire has paid Rs 3.7 crore on March 10 to the HVPNL for removing 32 high tension wires and electric poles but nothing has been done till date. Taking strong note of this, the court has directed the Managing Director of HVPNL to remain present on the next date of hearing. The MD has been directed to explain as to why the penal interest should not be recovered from his pocket.

The court also warned the contractor and concessionaire to give complete list of problems being faced by it in completing the Kalka-Pinjore-Parwanoo bypass. "Don't give us peace meal information and don't think that we don't understand your tactics to delay the case," the court observed.

Heading: Ankur’s ton puts Delhi in command on day 1 - Indian Express
Content:
While wheat sowing is in full swing in Punjab, there are reports of shortage of diammonium phosphate (DAP) fertilizer.

According to Dr A.S. Sidhu, head of the Department of Soils, the Punjab government has arranged triple super-phosphate (Triple) which is freely available. The phosphorus content in DAP and Triple is the same, said Dr Sidhu, as he advised the farmers to drill 65, 55 and 45 kg Triple per acre in low, medium and high phosphorus status soil, respectively.

As per the PAU recommendations, full doze of phosphorus and potash and half dose of urea is to be applied at the time of sowing and the remaining urea with first irrigation, in wheat. The timely sowing of wheat ensures higher grain yield, said Dr Sidhu, adding that farmers should sow wheat at the earliest using triple superphosphate in the absence of DAP.

The fertilizer, DAP contains 18% nitrogen and 46% phosphorus while Triple contains 46% phosphorus only. When we apply DAP, the nitrogen dose is reduced equivalent to 20 kg urea per acre, said Dr Sidhu. In case of triple superphosphate, the nitrogen dose is not reduced. Therefore, if triple superphosphate is to be used, farmers are advised to apply urea at 130 kg, 110 kg and 90 kg per acre in fields testing low, medium and high in nitrogen statuses, respectively.

Heading: School National Games camps from Nov 12 - Indian Express
Content:
Opener Ankur Julka (101) scored splendid ton to help Delhi post a respectable total of 248 runs on the first day of the match against Haryana in the C K Nayudu U-22 (North Zone) tournament being held at Sector 16 Stadium in Chandigarh on Friday.

Winning the toss Delhi skipper Rahul Yadav decided to bat first on a good track which had had bounce and pace. Haryana medium-pacers failed to take advantage of the moisture present in the atmosphere and kept balling short-pitched deliveries as well as on the outside the off stump. Openers Ankur and Abhishek were involved in the 61 runs partnership for the first wicket before Abhishek was removed by Chanderpal Saini. Heading: A tinge of lemon - Indian Express
Content:
Defending champions New Public School, Sector 18 boys' and girls' teams were dethroned in the fifth Emily Gosain Memorial Inter-School Basketball Tournament held at St Xavier's School, Sector 21 on Friday.

Playing an inspired game, St Xavier's School, Sector 44, Chandigarh wrested the boys' title while St Kabir School, Sector 26, Chandigarh stunned them in the girls' section.

St Xavier's-44 carved out a thrilling 64-52 verdict over New Public School in the boys' final while St Kabir School proved too good for NPS by routing them with an authentic margin of 55-16 in the one-sided girls' final. NPS felt the absence of their star player Smiti who suffered injury in their earlier match.

Defending champions NPS boys began on a whirlwind fashion by winning the first quarter by 18-7. However, St Xavier's boys were not discouraged. They reorganised their game and won the second quarter by 13-6. The half time score was 24-20 in favour of New Public School.

At the conclusion of the third set St Xavier's led by a narrow margin of one point (37-36). The thrilling third set saw both teams equal at 32-all. A three-pointer basket by Stanzin made 35-32 and Xavier's star player Gurjot (18) sunk a basket to give his team a lead by 37-36.

Despite midway through the last quarter Gurjot came out after committing five individual fouls, Xavier's continued to maintain pressure and slowly kept on increasing their margin. Vishwadeep (16), Anmol (12) and pint-sized three-point specialist Stanzin (9) systematically controlled the match. From 45-40 they increased their lead to 64-52. At one stage., NPS' main playmaker Sartaj (30) was rested for some time which gave an advantage to their rivals.

New Public School took the court without injured Smiti in the girls final. Absence of Smiti who had capitalised on rebounds in their earlier matches, was badly felt today. However, credit should not be taken away St Kabir School which played as a joint team. The deadly duo of Naina (23) and Rupandeep (20) demolished the NPS defence.

Heading: turning over - Indian Express
Content:
Like the fruit they are named after, Lemon Tree Hotels are fresh and energetic. Located opposite Wipro in Hinjewadi, Lemon Tree Hotel, Pune belongs to the chain of Lemon Tree Hotels in India. The ambience and reflected lightings in the restaurant create a soothing atmosphere. What grab the attention of the visitors the first time they visit the place are the ponytail hairstyles of the staff members. "It is official here. Managers and above have to maintain this hairstyle her," says Rupesh Singh, manager.

The passage to the restaurant is filled with humourous one-liners and funny quotes that make you forget the worries and enjoy the dining. But other than the soothing ambience and the pleasing services what is also attractive and easier for the wallet is the menu card at Lemontree. While the chef serves a variety of cuisine like Chinese, continental, Punjabi and so on, what is a favourite amongst the customers is the unlimited biryani offer that runs in the hotel after midnight.

"We are located in Hinjewadi and most of opur customers are software professionals or BPO employees. Considering the fact that they work round the clock, it is important that they get quality food but at an affordable price. And the response is overwhelming," says Singh. The chef explains saying, "We serve Hyderabadi Biryanis here but with a special touch of our own. While choice is limited for the vegetarians, non-vegetarians can select from a variety of biryanis. Under this offer, we offer unlimited biryani, salad, soup and a dessert at Rs 150."

While waiting for the food to get ready, one can enjoy the funny one-liners written on the tablecloth as well. The hospitality and service is truly world class. The hotel also offers multi-cuisine dining, a bar, recreation and fitness facilities, a swimming pool as well as a business centre, meeting rooms and state-of-the-art conference halls. Other services include 24x7 reception, housekeeping, laundry and room service. With unexpectedly reasonable prices in almost all the services that they offer, Lemon Tree Hotel definitely adds a new twist to one's visit every time.

Heading: Meal ticket - Indian Express
Content:
Fattoush

(pronounced as fa-thoosh)

Many good things have come out of the Levant and none is tastier or healthier than the Fattoush, a Lebanese salad made of vegetables and fried or toasted pieces of pita bread. The great thing about this salad is that it is flexible and the preparation time is minimal. Another upside of this dish is that it allows for the use of stale bread, which would otherwise be thrown out. Just toss together some seasonal vegetables and herbs according to taste and you have a fabulous and low-calorie salad. But for authenticity's sake it's best to stick to the mandatory ingredients, which include cucumbers, scallions, tomatoes, lettuce and day-old pita bread which is to be toasted until its brown. For the dressing, whisk together some extra-virgin olive oil, lemon juice and black pepper. If you're feeling too lazy to concoct this at home, troop to Souk at the Taj Mahal Palace and Tower, Apollo Bunder, or tuck into this Mediterranean delight at the Mabruk at Sahara Star, Santa Cruz.

Heading: Over 19 mills yet to get nod for cane crushing from commissionerate - Indian Express
Content:
Chef Wong takes you on a culinary journey through flavours, spices and tastes, courtesy the schezwan food festival in the city

Cuisine tales coming from expert palates often make our taste buds clamour for unknown tastes. Gauging this need of food lovers, Whispering Bamboo at hotel Taj Blue Diamond has come up with a schezwan special food festival — Schezwan Fever. The food fiesta introduces schezwan specialties of Master chef Wong Wen, who specialises in schezwan cuisine and is the latest member of the Chinese kitchen of Taj Blue Diamond.

Having won accolades for his expertise in schezwan delicacies back home in Beijing, Wong is all geared up to make Puneites develop a liking for schezwan food. "I want that whenever someone thinks of schezwan food, hotel Taj Blue Diamond should become the ultimate destination," says 25-year-old Wen.

Talking of his decision to come to India he says,"My teacher who works as a chef in Chandigarh was always full of praise for this country. So it didn't take me long to take a decision when I got an offer from Taj Blue Diamond" adds he.

A perfectionist by nature, Wong does not like to compromise on the condiment requirements of a particular dish. For him good food is that which has the best ingredients, is presented well and is served hot to guests. Like all other chefs, he also shares the opinion that guest satisfaction is the ultimate parameter of a good chef. "From Crunchy Water Chestnut and Baby Corn Wild Pepper to Crispy Pomfret Schezwan Style, Sliced Duck In Black Bean Chilli Sauce, Ladyfinger Black Bean Sauce and ultimately pamper the sweet tooth with toffees and pancakes, I serve everything," says he.

An expert hand at cooking Schezwan food for eight years does not deter him from relishing other cuisines. "Apart from Chinese, Indian and Italian dishes are my favourites. In fact I have developed a liking for butter chicken and rice," chuckles Wen. Interestingly the Chinese chef feels that Chinese food in India is as good as it is back home.

"Indian people and Indian food are lovely," are the words Wong does not shy away from repeating intermittently. Sitting with a translating machine as well as people who can make him understand English, an ecstatic Wen concludes in Chinese, "I may not be good at English language but I am good at my cooking skills and I love my work."

The festival on till November 16.

Heading: Sardar Dastur team to represent state in national championships - Indian Express
Content:
Owing to shortage of cane supply in the state, over 19 sugar mills in Maharashtra are yet to get permission for crushing cane from the state sugar commissionerate in the city. Due to the short supply of cane this season, the commissionerate has not permitted mills to transport cane outside the state. Instead, it is encouraging mills to bring more cane from outside.

Nearly 154 mills in the state have applied for permission to begin crushing cane this season. Senior officers from the sugar commissionerate said that the availability of cane is less than 50 per cent in around 19 mills and they have not been granted permission to begin crushing.

The officers said that some of the mills had even come forward stating that they had made alternate arrangements. "Local inquiry will be conducted to check the availability of cane," said an officer. He said that with a shortfall of 30 lakh tons of sugar production in 2008-09 as against 770 lakh tons of cane that was crushed last season, they expected around only 530 lakh tons to be crushed this season. "Sugar production is likely to come down to 62 lakh tons as against 91 lakh tonnes last season," he said.

The commissionerate also has noticed the trend of farmers to move towards other cash crops such as soyabean. "Last year, there was a diversion of around 15 per cent to 20 per cent in acre towards other crops. This year, we are yet to get the final figures," he said. According to the data available with the ministry of agriculture, the sugarcane-cultivated area in Maharashtra has dropped to 7.88 lakh hectares as against 10.88 lakh hectares in the previous season.

So far, around 17 mills have begun crushing and 2.50 lakh tons of cane has been crushed yielding a production of 22,000 tons of sugar with an average recovery of 9 per cent, said a member of the Maharashtra State Co-op Sugar Factories Federation (MSCSFF).

Heading: Now, commuters can complain against auto drivers refusing to ply - Indian Express
Content:
A petition committee of the Rajya Sabha has strongly recommended that persons affected with leprosy should be given a monthly maintenance allowance of Rs 2,000 and that they should be given a disability certificate irrespective of the degree of disability.

Dr S D Gokhale of the International Leprosy Union along with members including Dr P K Gopal of IDEA India and Uday Thakar of Hind Kusht Nivaran Sanghatana had jointly made a petition to the petition committee of the Rajya Sabha appealing for the formulation of a national policy for the empowerment and rehabilitation of leprosy affected persons.

The committee visited Hyderabad, Tirupati, Nelore, Chengalpattu, Chennai and Mumbai and met the affected persons. The committee visited 700 self settled colonies with a population of 70,000 leprosy patients. The committee has strongly recommended that the survey of leprosy patients should be taken up again and the Panchayat Raj institutions should also be associated with the survey.

There is also a need for socio-economic rehabilitation and empowerment of these persons and the committee felt that the discriminatory provisions in various Acts have hampered the process of empowerment of these people. The committee has also recommended that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in coordination with the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting should launch a nationwide campaign for advocating the curability of the disease.

The committee also urged the government to take up a plan of action and implement it in coordination with the state governments towards the welfare of the leprosy patients.

Heading: ACB wants to file corruption cases against  PMC men; civic body looks to GB for consent - Indian Express
Content:
Taking note of complaints from commuters against autorickshaws refusing to ply, the Regional Transport Authority (RTA) has decided to spread awareness among autorickshaw drivers in a campaign beginning next week.

"We will be joined by autorickshaw unions, the traffic police and some RTO officers where we will visit major autorickshaw stands and talk to the auto drivers about the rules of ferrying passengers. We will explain to them the repercussions of refusing passengers," said Baba Shinde, RTA member.

In the past two months, the RTO and the RTA have received around 450 complaints, out of which 187 auto rickshaw drivers have been booked. "These complaints include refusal to ply short distances, over charging and misbehaviour with passengers, Shinde said.

The RTA has published over 15,000 small pocket cards with information on the penalties for an autorickshaw driver for several offences. These will be distributed among auto drivers during the campaign. For the first time offence, the fine is Rs 500 and suspension of licence for 10 days, the second time offence will cost an auto driver Rs 1,500, the third time will cost the auto driver Rs 2,500 and his permit will be taken away.

Complainants can even post their complaints with the following information: vehicle registration number, time at which the passenger hired the vehicle, nature of the offence, address of the complainant (which will be kept confidential).

Heading: UoP’s gerontology course targets senior citizens - Indian Express

Civic body proposes to waive fees for backward class students

The civic administration has tabled a proposal before the standing committee to completely waive off the school fees for the students hailing from backward classes and studying in PMC-run English medium schools.

Following a demand from the Republican Yuva Morcha, the civic school board had asked the PMC for permission to waive off the fees. The school board had passed a resolution to this effect in its meeting in October. As per the proposal, students in English medium kindergartens have to pay Rs 90 per month, while it is Rs 150 per month for the students between Std I and VI. The quantum of backward class students in kindergarten is 1,335, the total fees amount to Rs 14.41 lakh, while the number in primary schools is 1,257 and their total annual fees amount to Rs 22.62 lakh.

Heading: UoP to host SAMPADA 2008 - Indian Express
Content:
If you are a senior citizen looking for detailed information on issues related to ageing, then the course on gerontology — started by the University of Pune (UoP) and International Longevity Centre (ILC), a voluntary organisation — may be just right for you. Gerontology is the science that deals with ageing and problems of aged persons.

"This is a first-of-its-kind course in the state and is aimed at empowering senior citizens through classroom teaching and practical training," said Anjali Raje, Deputy executive Director of the ILC.

Dr Narendra Jadhav, UoP Vice Chancellor said that with this course, the university will be in a position to keep a record of professional caregivers and act as an agency for the same. "This course is a preamble to the international conference on geriatrics that will be conducted next year as part of UoP's diamond jubilee function," he said. The three-month course will cover every aspect of ageing — health, hygiene, emotional balance, money management and laws. "Some of the modules include healthy dietary practices with demonstrations of recipes, personal hygiene and self-care, national policies related to senior citizens and overview of demography," Raje said.

The syllabus has been framed by UoP's school of health sciences and ILC and will be taught in Marathi. The admissions for the course, which is will begin on December 8, are on and will continue till first week of December. "The admissions will be given on first-come-first-served basis. There are 40 seats for the course. Although, anyone above 18 years of age is eligible for the course, we shall prefer senior citizens," Raje said.

The course will also include journal submission, short assignments, field visits to old age homes and group discussion. "While there will be no written examination, students will be evaluated on their participation in these activities," Raje said.

Dr Anita Kar of UoP's school of health sciences said that they have already received 18 enquiries for the course, all by senior citizens.

Heading: After CYG spat, Pawar and Kalmadi to share dais - Indian Express
Content:
Scientists from China, Japan, Europe and Singapore to attend

In an age when not many students opt for research in fundamental sciences, the second International Symposium on Advanced Materials and Polymers for Aerospace and Defence Applications (SAMPADA) 2008 to be held in December in the city, is expected to motivate students.

Apart from technical deliberations by the delegates, the conference will see international scientists from China, Japan, Europe, Indonesia and Singapore. It will also have open lectures for students of X, XI and XII on physics and mathematics.

Dr Narendra Jadhav, Vice Chancellor of University of Pune (UoP) — which will host the conference held from December 8 to 12 — said, "This conference will also pave way for collaborative international research," he said.

The conference will have 200 paper presentations, 150 of which are from India. There will be three plenary sessions, three key note speeches, presentations by product specialists. "Students will also get an opportunity to give oral presentation during this session," said Dr Rohitkumar Vora, chairman of the conference.

Professor Shankar Patil, head of physics department of UoP said that while the faculty is capable to interact with international scientists and update themselves, "this is a rare opportunity for students to interact with international scientists." Delegates from Department of Navy, USA, Department of Air Force, USA and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) will attend the conference.

The theme of the conference is 'Emerging trends in advanced materials' that will cover high performance and smart materials, speciality chemicals and polymer materials, multi-compositional and nano materials, design, synthesis, characterisation, processing, engineering and reliability testing methodologies and technology in defence and aerospace and intellectual property (IP) of state-of-the-art materials, polymers and technologies.

The conference is jointly organised by Materials Research Society of India (MRSI), Department of Physics of UoP, Centre for Materials for Electronics Technology (C-MET), National Chemical Laboratory (NCL), Defence Institute of Advanced Technology (DIAT), Asian Office of Aerospace Research and Development -Tokyo, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Department of Air Force, USA, Office of Naval research Global (ONR-Global), Science and technology, Department of Navy, USA, Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Reliance Industries Limited.

Before that, Pawar will formally kick start the construction work of Gurunam Academy, a hostel facility to be raised by the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) at Bombay Engineering Group (BEG), for the children of jawans, who have attained martyrdom. MLA Chandrakant Chhajed, Lt Gen Noble Thamburaj and mayor Rajlaxmi Bhosale will attend the function.

The last time that Pawar and Kalmadi had shared a stage was in December last year at the bhoomipujan ceremony of the Kasewadi slums where Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh was also present. At that function, Pawar had refrained from speaking citing that the function had been hijacked by the Congress.

Later, just before the CYG event and the inauguration of subway in Balewadi, Pawar had criticised Kalmadi for hogging the limelight for CYG.

"Despite being rejected by the citizens in the last municipal elections in Pune and Pimpri-Chinchwad, some people (Kalmadi) have not yet matured. People pulled them (Congress) out of power, but I don't understand how many more jolts will they need to grow up," Pawar had said.

Heading: Dow probe report faces delay - Indian Express
Content:
Tata Motors will keep shut its commercial vehicle plant in Pimpri from November 21 to November 26, due to a slump in demand.

The move follows a block closure of the Jamshedpur plant from November 6 to November 8, and the removal of 2,500 temporary employees over the past few months.

The Pimpri plant produces heavy commercial vehicles, light commercial vehicles, cars and utility vehicles. A statement said "unavailability of finance, coupled with high interest rates, is forcing customers to postpone purchases. Different segments of automobile industry have been impacted at different levels."

Under the shadow of a global recession, sales in the company's commercial vehicles unit dropped 29 per cent as it sold 19,514 vehicles in the domestic market this October as compared to 27,103 in October last year. Sale of medium and heavy commercial vehicles also witnessed a decline by 48 per cent and the light commercial vehicles by 10 per cent.

Debasis Ray, head, corporate communications, said the changed situation "will call for appropriate action from Tata Motors from time to time to match production with demand and avoid unnecessary buildup of inventory in the company or with the company's dealers".

On the axing of temporary employees, Ray said, "As per production demand we regularly engage and disengage temporary employees. All employees whose services have been disengaged were temporaries. This is a regular exercise."

The HCV unit of the Pimpri plant employs 7,500 people while the LCV unit has 2,500 employees. When asked about the status of permanent employees, Ray said, "There would be no layoffs."

At present, many departments in the company are working in one or two shifts.

Tata Motors Employees Union president Sujit Patil said temporary employees are usually engaged for a period of seven months after which they are removed. On the closure of the plant for about a week, Patil said, "We know about the block closure but have yet to receive a written communication from the company. Block closures have happened earlier too. It happens even for maintenance of machinery. The company can go in for block closure for 12 days a year."

The company has stated that the passenger car plant will work normally though.

Heading: Kidnap mystery: brigadier vanishes and resurfaces - Indian Express
Content:
The probe report on the Dow Chemicals imbroglio could miss its deadline with a demand being made that the head of the panel be replaced.

The SP Kurudkar-led committee was set up on October 19 and was to submit its report in a month.

But sources close to those crusading against the project alleged that Kurudkar was a close relative of an advocate working for the company. They are confident that he will be replaced.

"We have reported to the Union government his closeness to the committee. We have been assured that the committee would be re-constituted under a new head," said a member of the Warkari sect.

The sect has been campaigning for the removal of the project from Shinde village. They believe the project would pollute the environment. The government set up the committee to assess the project's environmental impact.

The three-member committee included IIT Bombay scientist Dr SK Gupta and a Groundwater Survey and Development Authority (GSDA) officer from Pune, SB Khandale. Member secretary of the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) Sanjay Khandare is secretary to the committee.

Heading: Keralites’ wishes take flight on Paramount’s wings - Indian Express
Content:
A retired brigadier, Shreechand Acchtani (63) of Kondhwa, was allegedly kidnapped on Wednesday before he reappeared on Thursday morning. Four unidentified persons had allegedly kidnapped him for a ransom of Rs 20 lakh and then released him. His reappearance remains as mysterious as his disappearance.

Police were unable to record Acchtani's statement as he was admitted to the Intensive care unit of Command Hospital in Wanavdi on Friday morning. Crime branch teams were hunting for the kidnappers.

"It was a case of kidnapping. Investigations are on and we cannot share the details now," said Deputy Commissioner of Police (crime) Anil Kumbhare.

Police sources said the kidnappers might have manhandled Acchtani, due to which he was in trauma. When The Indian Express visited Acchtani's house in Konark Puram at Kondhwa, he had been shifted to the Command Hospital under police protection.

Two policemen were deployed near his residence. At the hospital, Acchtani's wife said he would be under observation for two days at the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). "We are not in a position to speak to the media," she said.

The crime branch was clueless on why the kidnappers had released Acchtani. Police would be speaking to Acchtani after he recovers.

Acchtani, who had retired from the army some eight years ago, was a visiting faculty at prominent colleges in Pune. He taught business ethics. After giving a lecture at an institute in Hinjewadi, he was returning home by car via Katraj-Dehu bypass road, when four Hindi-speaking men allegedly kidnapped him.

They called his wife on the mobile phone and demanded Rs 20 lakh for his release. His wife informed police. Meanwhile, the kidnappers kept on calling his wife for money. They kept changing locations too. They asked his wife to reach various places in Satara district and then at Hadapsar, Wakad and Jejuri. While the crime branch teams were busy tracing the calls, the kidnappers released Acchtani at Katraj and escaped. Acchtani reached home safe.

Police did not record his statement as he was in a state of shock.

Heading: Change reaction - Indian Express
Content:
A long-standing appeal of the four-and-a-half lakh Keralites in the city seems to have been heard. Paramount Airways will soon launch trips between Pune and Thiruvananthapuram, connecting southern Kerala to Pune, via Chennai.

Pune will be the third centre in the western region for the airline, having recently started flights to Ahmedabad and Goa. According to Pune airport director Chandra Mauli, "The airport authorities had a meeting with Paramount officials on Friday, during which the airline proposed to set up flights to Pune. They plan to begin this month".

C R Kanan, vice president, Paramount Airways (Chennai operations), declined to comment. "We will formally announce our expansion plans at a news conference soon," he said. Interestingly, while other airlines are busy reducing costs and sectors, the contrast in the Indian aviation sector is striking.

"Although the information is not official, new flights to Pune have been planned. We intend to start by December 12, when direct trips from Chennai will be available along with via-flights from southern hubs like Thiruvananthapuram, Kochi, Madurai and Coimbatore. The base cost is likely to be Rs 999," said an airlines source.

"We have been campaigning for the last five years for air connectivity between Pune and Kerala. This step will help the four-and-a-half lakh Keralite residents of the city and the 2000-odd Keralite industrialists in Pune who need to frequently fly to and fro, apart from tourists and other travellers," said P C Nambiar, chairman, advisory council, Pune Malayalee Federation (PMF).

"We have been holding discussions with Paramount officials for the last two years and met them early this year. A month back, they assured us that flights will take off from Pune to Thiruvanthapuram. We have put forth a petition for a Pune-Mangalore-Kochi flight, which will be able to connect the entire southern belt," said PMF member Hari Narayan.

Reiterating this viewpoint, Nambiar said "When Paramount starts flights to Thiruvananthapuram, things will be easy for those headed to south Kerala from Pune, but travellers to north Kerala will still find the going tough as it takes 15 to 16 hours for the rest of the journey, given that Kerala's geographical stretch is long," said Nambiar.

Heading: Tribute to a legend - Indian Express
Content:
So what are Puneites cutting down on to make sure their budgets do not go awry in the wake of the economic recession? Read on

Plunging stock market, double-digit inflation, liquidity crunch, freezing recruitment and industry slowdown. The above have become the most oft-repeated words these days with global financial crisis and economic slowdown not leaving anyone untouched. Be it financially or psychologically. Be it a big corporate firm or a salaried individual. Be it a US citizen or a Puneite. No wonder that this year, even Diwali was lacking the usual lustre. The fear of recession is gripping everyone and there is a swift change in the spending habit of Puneites who till now had been labelled as big splurgers.

For Rahul Varma, an IT professional, it was a conscious decision. Says Varma, "My wife and I are shopaholics and we used to spend lavishly on clothes, movies, dining out and furniture. But I guess it's time to keep such impulsive expenses on hold. Earlier I used to book an air-ticket to a nearby city like Hyderabad also. But today, I will think twice about how important is the trip and I may consider going by train also."

Its not just the companies who are taking cost-cutting measures, its happening on the individual front also. Yashwant Bhogade, program manager, Infosys, says, "Looking at the gloomy situation in US and India, I have become a bit more calculative in terms of expenses. For instance, I spend around Rs 8000-9000 only on petrol every month. I plan to cut costs here."

Walking on the same path is Shadab Siddiqui, an e-commerce professional. "My attitude towards money and the expenditure has changed a lot because of the volatility in the market. I am cutting down on unnecessary expenses. Like earlier I used to use my four-wheeler to go to a closeby market also, but nowadays I am mostly using my motorbike. I am planning to continue this cost-cutting habit till I am confident about the market," says he.

There are also people who think that this whole change in the spending habit is more a psychological thing than logical. Says Shilpa Kulkarni, executive director, Aress Software, "I believe that most people have a rough idea of what is happening globally. I don't think that everybody is following the actual facts and figures. On a personal level I have not taken any precautionary steps but yes, I may in the near future. As it is it's human nature to get affected with what is happening around you and you tend to follow what others are doing, consciously or subconsciously."

Whether it is inflation or just a fear of recession, everybody can feel the heat. Nilesh Gothi, a dealer of white goods, Ankur Electronics, says, "As a businessman I have not yet experienced any significant downward growth in terms of sales volume. Although I have noticed a sharp decline in the number of customers visiting the showroom." But he agrees that there is a fear in the air and situation might be bad in the near future. Adds he, "To be on the safer side, we have decided not to stock more products and are cutting down on various expenses like bonus. Also there are no expansion plans in the coming days."

Nobody knows where the market or economy will head from here. But looks like, for the time being Puneites will stay away from the multiplexes, shopping malls, jewelers and of course the stock market!

Heading: Moral of the story - Indian Express
Content:
A classical music event has been organised by disciples of late Pandit C R Vyas to commemorate his birth anniversary

In a tribute to one of the greatest exponents of Hindustani classical vocals, late Pandit C R Vyas, established and upcoming stars of Indian classical music will perform a two-day-event of Indian classical music today and tomorrow at Y B Chavan Auditorium, Kothrud.

"Pandit C R Vyas passed away in 2002 and we have been organising this event since then. On his birth anniversary every year, we invite artistes from different genres of Indian Classical music and this time it is Satish Vyas, Rashid Khan, Vasundhara Komakali and so on," says Narendra Shah, Pancham Nishad Creative Ltd, the organisers.

Scheduled to begin today at 6.30 pm, the event will begin with the santoor concert by Satish Vyas, son of late pandit C R Vyas accompanied by Mukund Raj Deo on tabla. The first session will conclude with the vocal recital by the renowned vocalist ustad Rashid Khan. The morning session tomorrow will commence with the flute recital by Rupak Kulkarni and will be concluded by the veteran vocalist Vasundhara Komakali. The evening session will commence with the vocal performance by young talented vocalist Sanjeev Chimmalgi. L Subramaniam accompanied by his son Amby Subramanium will conclude the two-day festival.

Pandit Chintaman R Vyas, who passed away on January 10, 2002 in Kolkata at the age of 78, was a maestro of khayal. His style was an amalgamation of Kirana, Gwalior and Agra gharanas. "My father never differentiated between a disciple and son. He always used to say, do your work sincerely and you will automatically get the results. Today classical music is moving towards commercialisation. But we need to create a balance between old school of thoughts and modernisation. We have been organising this programme with the sole motive to promote Indian classical music. And we are happy with the kind of response that we have got over these six years," says Pandit Subhash Vyas, eldest son and disciple of pandit C R Vyas.

Heading: Come one, come all - Indian Express
Content:
Cinema needs to have a universal appeal irrespective of its origin, feel the screenplay writers

It was the discussion of ideas and explanation of a narrative as two eminent screenplay writers told the tale of storytelling. An open discussion on storytelling in Indian and German cinema gave way to sharing of experiences and opinions by the German filmmaker Horst Sczerba and screenplay writer Anjum Rajabali.

Organised by the Film and Television Institute of India and University of Pune in association with the Max Muller Bhavan, the workshop had talks on the various ways of storytelling In India, Germany and across the globe. Speaking on universal storytelling Rajabali says, " The cultural practices might differ in each country but any story can be understood universally if the conceptualisation is appropriate and if it can help identify with the story. The increasing cross-cultural professional engagements and practitioners' and experts' answers to the issues of cross-cultural differences are leading to universal cinema. Story telling should be universally understood. Because it is presented in a way larger than life, many people are perhaps not able to relate to it but a co relation can put cultures together."

Sczerba feels that to direct a film it is extremely essential to thoroughly have seen or experienced the concept shown in the film. "Every story in each set up or a country has certain essentials. I am not sure if an Indian can direct a German film or vice versa because of our unawareness of many things in the respective countries. Even in Germany, we have differences of lower class and upper-class. If someone who does not distinguish the two classes makes a film, it is a cliché of another cliché which is not authentic.I can't even direct a German movie if I am not convinced of the place or the person mentioned because as a director I am keen on authentic characters. If cinema can happen with the coming together of people from various countries, it's a wonderful chance to create a new language but lets make sure that the language is authentic," adds Sczerba.

The filmmaker has also been holding workshops for students of screenplay writing in the city. Speaking on the lesser popularity of German cinema as compared to Hollywood in his country he says, "Hollywood is more popular in Germany since we do not have enough funds to match their technical superiority. Before we shoot, the aspect of budget and affordability questions a film's materialisation. This makes the American movies rule almost 95 per cent of the theatrical scene and with around 150 thousand audience it is quite difficult to retrieve the money for any German producer. We have amazing stories but its difficult to do something like Star Wars. There are many small budget successful films but ultimately that is not business."

However, in India, the scenario is opposite according to Rajabali who says, "In India too there are specific difficulties in cinema making. We cannot have cultural partiality. But cinema in India comes from the existing story telling traditions that we are immensely attached to, what we see on the screen is reminiscent of our own story telling method. That makes the Hindi film industry define storytelling in our country leaving no room for the Hollywood films to compete."

Heading: Questions in Israel - Indian Express
Content:
Almost two months after the Delhi Jal Board (DJB) inaugurated the first ePay Automated Bill Payment Kiosk to increase consumer convenience, the payment of water bills has become an ordeal for residents of Hari Nagar, many of whom are senior citizens.

Residents say bills reach them only two days before the last date for payment or even later. People start queuing up outside the solitary counter at the office from 8 am — the official opening time is 9 am.

"We queue up as early as 8 am. The officials, however, don't turn up before 9.30. Then they take at least half-an-hour to clean up the office," Raj Chopra, a 70-year-old resident of Subhash Nagar said. She says it's difficult for her to stand in queue for hours without any shade or water to drink.

It doesn't help that residents from several adjoining areas like Meenakshi Garden, Mayapuri, Maya Enclave and Rajouri Garden also come to pay their water bills at the DJB office in Hari Nagar.

Satish Kumar (61), a resident of Hari Nagar, says officials would open two more counters to collect bills earlier if there was a rush. "But now there is only one counter and at least 300 people in queue. There is a cheque drop box but it doesn't have a lock. We have no option but to keep waiting in this never ending queue," he says. "I have been coming here for the last two days to deposit my bill but had to go back seeing the long queue. But today is the last date and I have no other option," he says.

K L Gandhi (65), a heart patient, was also in the queue. "I reached here at 8.45 am to find that at least 60 people were already standing in queue. I don't know how long people like me can bear with such administrative apathy. It's a wait of at least three hours every time, with 300-400 people making a 1 km-long queue," Gandhi says.

The CM had also announced that ePay Kiosks would remain open 24 hours. "I once came on a lean day around 3 pm but the counter was closed much before its official time," Gandhi says.

Heading: Be well - Indian Express
Content:
After my first and hopefully not last visit to Israel, I can safely say it is God's own country. A cliché for sure but as most clichés are often accurate and true, this is the best way I can describe Israel.

We did a whirlwind tour that had us discover a myriad of miracles in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and areas around, leaving us sometimes emotionally drained to mouth-opening awe. My first flirtation however was not quite so enthralling. I was detained at the airport and questioned several times about my identity and whether I had any Muslim blood (sic).

After visiting the Holocaust museum and the Children's Memorial, the persecution against Jews seemed more cold-blooded than I had ever realised and I understood that life had not been beautiful at all 60 years ago and sadly not even now. Extremely agitated, I could feel my heart thumping like a percussionist beating on bongos. I learnt that it was a horrendous and torturous fantasy of a German doctor to inject the TB virus into children and then ruthlessly wipe out any remains, leaving not a trace of proof. This is one of the least harmful acts; the others are blood curling.

We saw the Dead Sea Scrolls that gave us the teachings of the Bible, the 14 stages of Christ, from being condemned to death to where his body lay in a tomb. The Wailing Wall beneath and the Jewish/Muslim/Christian/Armenian quarters make Jerusalem the king of all cities.

The markets were lively and the falafel delicious. King Herod's Masada Fort was architectural genius. Floating in the Dead Sea with a mud pack and a pre-sulphur bath was psychosomatically therapeutic. Watching Zubin Mehta conduct his much loved Israel Philharmonic (Puccini's Turendot) a pleasant windfall. We made it to Haifa to see the beautiful Bahai shrine, the Golan heights and even fit in Nazareth.

I stayed the night in Tiberias with the most spectacular view of the Galilee. After all the delicious Israeli wine, I was tempted to try my luck in the sea but what with my alarming consumption of kosher meat I knew I would most certainly sink.

The two places during my trip however have left me with a lot of unanswered questions, and sadly some can never be answered. For instance, a part of Jerusalem, Mea Sharim, where the Orthodox Jews live are waiting for their Messiah to salvage them.

While they wait, they are so steeped in their orthodoxy that they refuse to blend in with the rest of Israel. They'll be damned if you voice your faith in Christ and they (the men) will most certainly spit at you (the women) if you are indecently dressed (capris and a T-shirt).

After visiting the army and going to the dreaded border shared between Palestine and Israel, I had a glimpse of the children in the war room. There were 18-year-old girls scanning the computer for possible terrorists. Do not the Jews of Mea Sharim realise that these children are their Messiahs? They have thousands not one. These are God's children who go to war and leave their parents at the age of 18 who have seen their brothers and friends die or survive severely handicapped. They are out every night knowing they may never come back.

Do they not realise that if they do try and help, these children might be able to prevent their own children from being part of a war. The first prayer from every Israeli mother is to prevent her children from going to war. They don't dream of health, love, laughter. They live in constant fear, hoping their children never grow up so they can never be taken away by the army.

It frustrates me but I suppose there are some things the persecuted just can't forgive and forget. Maybe I don't blame the authorities for questioning me about Muslim blood.
