Pental had condemned the incident on Friday.

Heading: Missing votes for years, cops on poll duty finally get to elect their candidates - Indian Express
Content:
As many as 80 flights got delayed due to poor visibility at the IGI Airport on Saturday morning. Adding to the woes for passengers, the new Instrument Landing System (ILS) of the third runway, set up to assist landing and takeoff in low visibility, was found to have some fault due to which flights could not take off from the new runway.

Result: congestion on the existing runways due to the backlog.

"Normal visibility dipped to 650 meters in the morning while Runway Visibility Range (RVR) was around 1,000 meters. As a result, most of the arrivals and departures were delayed," an airport official said. Officials said delay in flights ranged between 30 minutes and four hours.

"An Indian Airlines flight, scheduled to arrive from Patna at 10.30 am, arrived at 2.35 pm," the IGI official said. "There was heavy backlog till evening; almost every arriving flight had to wait in the air."

With the ILS not working, some international arrivals were also delayed. The situation became somewhat brighter after 10.30 am, when visibility improved.

At a recent meeting of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) with airline representatives and airport authorities to tackle fog-related problems, it was decided that morning and evening peak hours would be slotted to airlines with compliant aircraft and trained pilots to operate flights in dense fog in near-zero visibility conditions.

Heading: Family in tow, V K files nomination - Indian Express
Content:
After spending years manning booths and security when the rest of the Capital dances the ballet of ballot, Delhi Police officials would be able to vote in these Assembly elections. Come November 27, and the men in khaki would be able to cast their vote through the postal ballot system.

Casting their votes two days before the rest of the city goes to the polls, their postal ballots would also be the first to be counted.

There are approximately 60,000 police officials in Delhi, of which approximately 50,000 are eligible to vote. But they were unable to vote till date since they were on election duty or routine patrolling, and the postal ballot system was not available for the Capital. An officer, who has not voted once in 30 years of service, said, "I live in Shalimar Bagh, and if patrolling duty falls at a polling booth in South Delhi, it leaves me no time to cast my ballot."

Besides the police personnel, polling officers of the Election Commission, teachers from government schools, MCD officials, election observers and other officials on election duty were also left with no option but to forego their voting rights till date.

There would be some 11,000 polling booths for Delhi's 70 Assembly seats this time. The five officials appointed by the Election Commission as polling officers in each of these booths also cannot vote. The total number of polling officers would be around 75,000, including officials from various government departments.

An Election Commission officer said the final list of the number of polling officers would be out soon.

The total number of votes that is usually not counted reaches up to 2 lakh, Election Commission officials said. Delhi has 1.07 crore voters on the electoral roll at present.

"For the first time, we have decided to make sure their (those on poll duty) votes are also cast through postal ballots. Votes of these officials are also important," Delhi's Chief Electoral Officer Satbir Silhas Bedi said.

Welcoming the new step, a police officer (name withheld on request) said, "I had heard of postal ballot but it was not implemented in Delhi till date. Now, finally, I can take part in choosing who leads my state. Every vote counts, and policemen are also citizens of Delhi."

Postal ballots have been used in several states earlier, though not in Delhi.

Heading: Karya Siddhi to get a ticket, Shatru Mardan to overpower rivals: astrologers sell in poll season - Indian Express
Content:
The day begain like any other for BJP's chief ministerial candidate V K Malhotra. Around 8:30, family members of BJP's chief ministerial candidate V K Malhotra, congregated for a havan. Malhotra was up by 6, did his pranayam, had a frugal breakfast of toast and milk, and joined in the havan led by wife Krishna Malhotra.

Later, he met scores of BJP workers. Today was his big day — he would be filing nomination papers at Jamnagar House on Shahjahan Road.

Around noon, Malhotra with wife Krishna, son Ajay, daughter-in-law Ruchi, daughter Anupama Malik, two grandchildren, Akshay (16) and Aditya (13) left for Jamnagar House. By the time they got there, the venue was already crawling with BJP workers in saffron caps and sashes who nearly blocked Shahjahan Road. The scene seemed all the more chaotic with the defeaning sound of drumbeats.

Top BJP leaders Arun Jaitley, Sushma Swaraj, Vijay Goel, Harsh Vardhan, Arti Mehra and Vijender Gupta were already waiting for Malhotra at additional district magistrate Bansh Raj's office. Akali Dal chief Prakash Singh Badal and his son Sukhbir Singh Badal were also present. Indian National Lok Dal chief Om Prakash Chautala and Punjabi folk singer Hans Raj Hans were among those present.

Malhotra filed his nomination around 12:35 pm after taking the customary oath.

"We performed a havan as it was my daughter Medha's birthday. We're confident of winning two-thirds majority in the Assembly elections. As my father is busy, I've already started meeting workers and residents in the area," Malhotra's son Ajay told reporters. Medha Malhotra is pursuing a course in designing at NID, Ahmedabad.

Other family members have also joined the campaigning. "My sister-in-law Ruchi and I carry out door-to-door campaigning for my father. This evening too, I'm organising an informal get-together to facilitate his meeting with residents of the area. I'm also managing his website, which will be inaugurated shortly," said Malhotra's daughter Anupama Malik, who lives in Panscheel Park. Malik is pursuing her PhD from IIT.

As soon as Malhotra' entourage cleared the courtyard, Samajwadi Party candidate Neelam Saxena came in with her followers to file nominations for the Greater Kailash seat.

Returning officer Bansh Raj has received one more nomination for GK from Jitender Kumar Gupta of the Bharatiya Pragatisheel Congress.

Meanwhile, several other BJP leaders too filed their nomination papers on Saturday, including senior leaders, Jagdish Mukhi and Harsharan Balli.

Heading: Cong yet to announce names of 22 candidates - Indian Express
Content:
Aspiring MLAs are not the only ones busy these days. Some of the city's renowned astrologers are equally busy. For them the peak season started much before the elections. "Politicians had started coming to me when internal planning was on. Then they wanted to know whether they would get a ticket. Now, they want to know what chances they have of winning," said astrologer Jai Govind Shastri.

Shastri said politicians come with their horoscopes. "Some want to know whether they would get a party ticket to contest the elections. Those who were sure of getting a ticket wanted to know whether or not they will win the seat," said Shastri.

Not all politicians have favourable 'stars'. "In case a politician's chances of winning are less, we perform a puja for assured success," said Acharya Krishan Dutt Shastri. "Our Vedic shastra has several mantras to assure victory and we perform pujas for them," said Acharya. Acharya also said these days his telephone is rings continously. "I have been getting calls till late in the night from politicians. Many of them believe in astrology," said Acharya.

Based on the position of stars the astrologers recommend solutions. Pujas like Shatru Mardhan and Virodi Shanti are performed to win over opponents.

"To help them win tickets, I had performed the Karya Siddhi puja for sevaral politicians. Almost all of them got tickets," said Jai Govind Shastri.

"Almost everybody gets a Rudrabhishek done. It helps them attract the public whenever they go for a public meeting. The puja ensures that they leave a lasting impact on the public," added Shastri.

Both Acharya and Shastri do not wish to reveal the names of the politicians. "I have performed pujas for those who were pitching for the chief minister's seat," said Acharya Krishna Dutt Shastri who also is the general secretary of the Akhil Bharitya Jyotish Parishad.

Star-gazing
* Karya Siddhi:To get the ticket
* Shartru Mardan: To defeat the enemy
* Virodhi Shanti: To defeat the enemy
* Rubrabhishek: To attract the public
* Mahamritunjaye : If Saturn and Jupiter are weak

Heading: VOTERS SPEAK: GB Pruthi - Indian Express
Content:
The Delhi Congress seems to have hit a deadlock over deciding on candidates for its remaining 22 seats. Sources claim AICC president Sonia Gandhi chaired a meeting of the election commitee attended by Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit, DPCC chief JP Aggarwal, AICC general secretaries Ahmed Patel and Ashok Gehlot to decide on the matter. While the list was to be declared on Saturday, party stalwarts could not arrive at a final decision and another meeting is slotted for Sunday on finalising the candidate for Deoli constituency in South Delhi.

Congress sources said the party is contemplating allotting the seat to former Union minister Buta Singh's son Harvinder Singh 'Lovely' which may stir opposition within the party. Meanwhile, Shadiram is expected to be alotted the Sadar Paharganj seat and Health Minister Yoganand Shastri's name has been finalised for Mehrauli. Minto Road sitting MLA Tajdar Babbar, backed by Ahmed Patel, is expected to get Jangpura, sources said.

Heading: At last, Noida draw over - Indian Express
Content:
Gurjjars hold sway
The BSP factor might be giving sleepless nights to the Congress, but for the BJP, the party spells good times. On Saturday, spreading cheer in the BJP camp, the BSP councillor from ward 99 in Tuglaqabad, Giri Raj, declared he would be joining the BJP. The BJP has given a ticket to Ramesh Bhiduri from the area, while the Congress has fielded Sheesh Pal. The BJP is at present confident of winning Tughlaqabad after fielding a Gurjjar candidate.

BJP's Tyagi from Burari
BJP has decided to stop playing the waiting game before deciding upon the candidate for Burari and declared local candidate Sri Krishan Tyagi as their man from the area.
Tyagi has been working for a long time in the area and also lives there.
BJP candidate for Gandhi Nagar, Kalpana Jain, has formally withdrawn her candidature. The party is yet to announce their candidate from Gandhi Nagar. With Jain's withdrawal, the BJP only has three women candidates now.

Heading: Stage set for Half Marathon - Indian Express
Content:
The Noida Authority will begin the process of transferring land to the allottees within a week after the draw of lots for allotment of 1,250 residential plots ended on Saturday.

Stopped by the court following alleged rigging in the last draw organised in July 2005, Noida Authority officials said the draw, which began this time on Wednesday, has selected 267 allottees for plots in the general category and 268 for reserve category plots measuring 450 sq m. Noida Authority deputy CEO N P Singh said some technical snags cropped up during allocation of land to a few allottees, and they will be allocated provisional land as per the Allahabad High Court's orders. Singh said the Authority has sent teams to procure land transfer forms. "Almost 97 per cent of the allottees will be able to get their plots by next week but a few have been allotted land provisionally as they have not submitted some of the documents needed," the deputy CEO said.

Successful candidates would have to submit 30 per cent of the total amount for their plots within 30 days. The Authority has also prepared a site plan of the land to be transferred to allotees to cut out meddling by middlemen.

But many who have found their names after the draw say the land rates are gone up a jot too steeply in the four years since the scheme was launched in 2004. "I will not be able to take possession of my plot," an allottee, who did not want to be named, said. "The rate of 450-square metre land I have received in the draw is Rs 1.75 crore. I cannot arrange so much money.

"I think the solution would be to surrender the land to the Authority itself."

The draw was carried out manually this time, as per High Court order, after the computerised draw of lots held in July 2005 was found to be rigged.

Heading: Book explores attitude towards dogs in mythology - Indian Express
Content:
Cricketers, film stars, athletes and politicians — all on one platform make a heady cocktail. But the star-studded field at the fourth edition of the Delhi Half Marathon is not merely about the pomp and show. It is about making Delhi's citizens aware of the importance of coming together, celebrating unity and running for more than one cause.

The star parade includes the likes of legendary cricketers Sir Richard Hadlee and Kapil Dev, heptathlete par excellence Jackie-Joyner Kersee, star couple Ajay Devgan and Kajol, Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor and music director A R Rahman. Beijing Olympic bronze medallists Vijender Singh and Sushil Kumar will of course be there to lend more weight.

They may be from different fields but if there is one feeling that unites all of them — physical fitness helps develop mental toughness. "To be mentally tough, one has to be physically fit. And together with discipline, everything falls into place," Sir Richard Hadlee says.

More than that, Sir Hadlee believes it is important to overcome a global problem like obesity. "These marathons actually help people in general, particularly youngsters, who are addicted to television and video games," he says.

But why he is here? "After being associated with cricket for 36 years, including 18 years of active playing career, I have given up the game. But at 57, I know how I can keep myself fit. Though I may not be running tomorrow, I want to associate myself with something different. By my association if I can bring more runners to the Delhi Great Run, I would have done my job," the legendary cricketer, the first to cross the 400-wicket mark, says.

For Jackie-Joyner it's all about giving back. "I do a lot of community service back home, and being part of the Delhi Half Marathon gives me another opportunity to help a cause — like the charity events that organisers Procam International hold diligently year after year."

And the actors, Vivek Singh of Procam says, add star value, being brand ambassadors of the event. 'It helps us raise funds for charity, apart from drawing people to the event," he says.

He says such events inculcate the habit of running among senior citizens, women and children. "Our idea is to motivate them to come and participate and develop the habit," his brother Anil Singh says.

As for the main event, the organisers have for the first time introduced two Kenyan runners called the 'Rabbits'. They will be pacemakers for the lead group that will see the Ethiopian, Kenyan, Russian and Indian athletes participate. Ian Ladbroke, the elite athletes' agent, says: "The Rabbits will help the runners clock a sub-60 minute timing for the 21.097 km distance." But the million dollar question is: Are the Indian runners prepared for it?

Heading: Lok Adalat disburses Rs 1.54 cr - Indian Express
Content:
If you think a dog's life, has always been just that, think again. Shedding new light on attitudes towards Indian dogs is a new book, which sets out to chronicle the several lives of the dog in Indian mythology.

Bringing together little known nuggets from folk tales, temple art, literature, Bibek Debroy says attitudes towards dogs in the subcontinent have varied over time and space.

In Delhi's Bhairava Temple for example, the tradition of worshipping dogs has a long and little known history. Debroy, who has an abiding interest in mythology, found several references to dogs while translating Hindu mythological texts, which prompted him to trace the changing status of the dog in various cultures and mythologies. His book Sarama and Her Children, draws its name from Sarama, the dog of god Indra mentioned in the Rig Veda and perceived ancestor from which all subsequent dogs have descended. He gave a talk on the book at the Indian Habitat Centre on Friday.

An economist and professor at the Centre for Policy Research by profession and dog lover, Debroy says, "Despite the existence of several perceptions of dogs in mythology, an antipathy towards dogs still seems to persist."

For instance, dogs were recognised for their utilitarian roles in herding, hunting, and as watchdogs in pre-Vedic and Vedic times. Dogs from the north western region were exported to Persia, with Alexander the great too having a fleet of Indian fighting dogs.

Debroy says that with changing social and economic conditions, and the decline of traditional Vedic gods like Indra, Yama and Rudra, along the corresponding rise in the status of Vishnu and the brahamanical tradition, there was a corresponding decline in the status of the dog. In the increasingly hierarchical society, the utilitarian status of dogs receded and the animal was now associated with the "lower" castes.

Dogs continued to be held in respect in the Shiva and Shakti traditions, the tantric tradition and Buddhism. A reflection of this is the persistence of dog worship in several Bhairava temples across India and Nepal.

Heading: Hari Nagar residents, senior citizens wait in long queues to pay bill at DJB e-pay kiosk - Indian Express
Content:
The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) Lok Adalat, organised on Saturday for the first time with a berth for a doctor on the bench, disposed of 47 per cent of the cases and received an encouraging response at all five district court complexes.

Organised by the Delhi Legal Services Authority (DLSA), more than Rs 1.54 crore was disbursed by the bench, comprising a sessions judge and an associate doctor, who aided victims and insurance companies arrive at harmonious decisions. While the sessions judge looked after legal issues and lawful ways of resolving contentious issues pertaining to compensation, the doctors opined about the nature of injuries and similar medical matters so as to arrive at a just and fair figure for compensation.

As many as 496 cases were listed at the specially constituted courts for the Lok Adalat at all the court complexes — Tis Hazari, Rohini, Karkardooma, Patiala House and Dwarka.

Various public and private insurance companies, involved in legal battles with victims, sent their representatives to the courts. This was also the first Lok Adalat to be organised company-wise, which certainly helped in reducing confusion among litigants and judicial officers.

In cases where documents were not complete, parties and companies opted for the cases to be heard by the same bench on December 13, when the next Lok Adalat will be organised.

"The exercise was fruitful and I am certain it helped all parties concerned. More such Lok Adalats will be organised in the future," Additional Sessions Judge Sunita Gupta, who presided over a bench at a Tis Hazari court, said.

Calling the event a step towards changing long-established notions regarding court proceedings, DLSA project officer Sanjay Sharma told Newsline, "It was an institutionalised effort to accord relief to the victims of motor accidents with minimal technicalities and hassles."

The continuous MACT Lok Adalats will definitely assist the DLSA achieve the object of providing "access to justice for all", so that justice was not denied to citizens because of economic reasons or other disabilities, Sharma said.

At Tis Hazari Courts

Jahri Devi

Jahri Devi's (65) son Rajesh Shah (24) was mowed down by a car in Rohini on September 4, 2006. He is survived by his wife and two daughters, aged four and six years.

"No amount of money can bring my son back. But at least I will be spared from running to court every now and then in the hope for a monetary reprieve that could help his two daughters study," she said.

Jahri Devi filed a claim petition at a Rohini Motor Accident Claims Tribunal the same year. Two years on, the court had barely concluded the recording of evidence.

On Saturday, the first continuous motor accident Lok Adalat, held at a district court complex, delivered the fair decision she had been hoping for. Her case was settled after Presiding Officer ASJ Dilbagh Singh helped her counsel and the representative from National Insurance Co Ltd reach an amicable decision and an award of Rs 4.90 lakh was finalised.

"I won't comment on the quantum of damages but now I at least know the money my son's family has in their hands will provide for a better future," Jahri Devi said.

Mukund Lal

Mukund Lal's (60) autorickshaw was hit from behind by a speeding car near ITO flyover on May 4, 2007. The autorickshaw overturned and his right leg came under the vehicle. Despite regular treatment, he could not stand without using crutches again and is still undergoing medication, hoping to walk on his own one day. Lal's MACT petition was pending at a Karkardooma court, from where the matter was recommended to the Lok Adalat for amicable settlement.

More than anything else, Lal wanted an end to his dates in court, as his physical infirmities posed great difficulties in attending regular proceedings. The Lok Adalat proceedings lasted barely 10 minutes, as Lal's counsel and son-in-law discussed the award money with the representatives of an insurance company. The judge acted as a catalyst and the matter was decided at Rs 1.90 lakh. Lal said he was "satisfied", as he did not want to get entangled into the court proceedings, which could have run on for a number of years. "I wanted immediate relief for continuing my treatment. If I can't walk, for how long could I fight in courts and be present on each and every date?" Lal said.

Heading: Trader from Allahabad shot at, is critical - Indian Express
Content:
After my first and hopefully not last visit to Israel, I can safely say it is God's own country. A cliché for sure but as most clichés are often accurate and true, this is the best way I can describe Israel.

We did a whirlwind tour that had us discover a myriad of miracles in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and areas around, leaving us sometimes emotionally drained to mouth-opening awe. My first flirtation however was not quite so enthralling. I was detained at the airport and questioned several times about my identity and whether I had any Muslim blood (sic).

After visiting the Holocaust museum and the Children's Memorial, the persecution against Jews seemed more cold-blooded than I had ever realised and I understood that life had not been beautiful at all 60 years ago and sadly not even now.

Extremely agitated, I could feel my heart thumping like a percussionist beating on bongos. I learnt that it was a horrendous and torturous fantasy of a German doctor to inject the TB virus into children and then ruthlessly wipe out any remains, leaving not a trace of proof. This is one of the least harmful acts; the others are blood curling.

We saw the Dead Sea Scrolls that gave us the teachings of the Bible, the 14 stages of Christ, from being condemned to death to where his body lay in a tomb. The Wailing Wall beneath and the Jewish/Muslim/Christian/Armenian quarters make Jerusalem the king of all cities.

The markets were lively and the falafel delicious. King Herod's

Masada Fort was architectural genius. Floating in the Dead Sea with a mud pack and a pre-sulphur bath was psychosomatically therapeutic. Watching Zubin Mehta conduct his much loved Israel Philharmonic (Puccini's Turendot) a pleasant windfall. We made it to Haifa to see the beautiful Bahai shrine, the Golan heights and even fit in Nazareth.

I stayed the night in Tiberias with the most spectacular view of the Galilee. After all the delicious Israeli wine, I was tempted to try my luck in the sea but what with my alarming consumption of kosher meat I knew I would most certainly sink.

The two places during my trip however have left me with a lot of unanswered questions, and sadly some can never be answered. For instance, a part of Jerusalem, Mea Sharim, where the Orthodox Jews live are waiting for their Messiah to salvage them.

While they wait, they are so steeped in their orthodoxy that they refuse to blend in with the rest of Israel. They'll be damned if you voice your faith in Christ and they (the men) will most certainly spit at you (the women) if you are indecently dressed (capris and a T-shirt).

After visiting the army and going to the dreaded border shared between Palestine and Israel, I had a glimpse of the children in the war room. There were 18-year-old girls scanning the computer for possible terrorists. Do not the Jews of Mea Sharim realise that these children are their Messiahs? They have thousands not one. These are God's children who go to war and leave their parents at the age of 18 who have seen their brothers and friends die or survive severely handicapped. They are out every night knowing they may never come back.

Do they not realise that if they do try and help, these children might be able to prevent their own children from being part of a war. The first prayer from every Israeli mother is to prevent her children from going to war. They don't dream of health, love, laughter. They live in constant fear, hoping their children never grow up so they can never be taken away by the army.

It frustrates me but I suppose there are some things the persecuted just can't forgive and forget. Maybe I don't blame the authorities for questioning me about Muslim blood.

Heading: When Barramundi Becomes Axis Mundi - Indian Express
Content:
Four armed robbers fired at a businessman and fled with his bag in crowded Nayi Sadak area of Central Delhi. Ashok Kumar Pal (39), is in a critical state in LN Hospital.

The police said Pal, an Allahabad-based businessman, had arrived at New Delhi Railway Station on the Prayag Raj Express with his friend Guddu. He flagged down a cycle-rickshaw from the railway station to go to New Lajpat Rai Market. "When the rickshaw reached Nayi Sadak around 7.45 am, four unidentified men on two black Pulsar motorcycles hit the rickshaw. Pal and Guddu fell on the road and two of the men tried to snatch Pal's bag. As Pal resisted, one of the attackers shot at him with a country-made pistol. The attackers then made off with his bag," a senior police officer said.

A crowd that had gathered tried to stop the assailants. One of the men then fired three rounds in the air and threatened to shoot anybody who stopped them. Guddu told the police the bag had some clothes, papers and a little cash. DCP, Central, Sagar Preet Hooda said, "A case of robbery has been registered and investigations are on."

Heading: Cheeky girls - Indian Express
Content:
If the sound of a blackened barramundi served with tiger prawns infused with Darjeeling tea is enough to tickle your taste buds, then half the battle is won. And by the time you have finished off the Aborigine-Indian fusion dish, you will understand what the Australian chef Sunny De Ocampo means when he says, "This is my way of saying hello to India. While I like my cooking to reflect the local culture and ingredients, the fish barramundi is an Australian delicacy that got its name because of its dark skin," Even as the succulent barramundi moistens the palate, the crunchy prawns provide the tang since the chef has lightly drizzled tamarind juice on them. At the Australian seafood promotion at Threesixty0, The Oberoi, the 34-year-old who specialises in seafood recipes and makes a mean Tasmanian salmon served on mascarpone rings, says, "Cooking is a reflection of my travels around the world." And there barramundi is often the axis mundi.

The festival is on till November16

Heading: Clean crusader - Indian Express
Content:
A band of three expat women cranks out saucy songs about crusty old friend and demanding wives

It's 2 in the afternoon and the girls are lounging in Liz Cotton's living room. An old piano rests in a corner and Cotton's cat scampers around as she casually strums the guitar, while two other women—Irit Namatinia and Sumana Bhasin—in their mid-thirties, like Cotton, sing a naughty song. No bittersweet pop or soul rock for this all-female band. Wotshelike, formed in 2006, cranks out saucy songs about delicious affairs, demanding expatriate wives and crusty old friends. Call them crass, but the songs will make you laugh your guts out.

Singer-songwriter-guitarist Cotton, a Britisher who formed the band and has been living in Delhi since 1998, has been composing comedy songs since she was six. "I was very active in the London comedy circuit where I sang songs and also wrote for a comedy sketch club. Then my husband got transferred to Pakistan, where the comedy scene is not as lively."

Cotton, who moved to India a decade ago, has a few gigs in Delhi to her credit. "I did gigs on my own in Delhi but thought it would be more fum performing comedy with an all-girl band," she says. After a concert in Shillong, she put up posters for audition. Soon, four women joined her and Wotshelike was formed. Namatinia, an expatriate who was brought up in Kenya has been in India since 2005. A jazz school graduate, Namatinia says, "We throw in a bit of action with our trademark props such as pink handcuffs and a swish fan." But the naughtiness and fun had a downside. The band has pared down to three. "We had an Australian who left as she found the songs too saucy for her taste" says Cotton.

The feisty Cotton has composed 15 songs so far for Wotshelike. "She writes the lyrics and sets them to music then we make a few changes later," says Bhasin, mother of two and a former member of Mrigya, an Indian fusion band she quit after the extensive tours took a toll on her. The songs are written largely from Cotton's experience. An old friend living in Pune is the subject of the song Granny Grab, about a respectable woman on a lookout for a dandy. The song goes like this: She'll never smile, she'll never frown. And it's not because she's not enjoying. But her face is full of botox, frozen in time. "well, she never missed my birthday," says Cotton with an impish smile. "And yes, she knows I made a song based on her," adds Cotton.

Some of the songs—like Hardship Posting and Ashram Chowk are peppered with Hindi words. Namatinia and Cotton took Hindi classes when they arrived in India, and they can now speak the language fluently. Wotshelike has performed at events, restro-bars like Live and Raga and plans are underway to cut an album. "Next, I would like to go to Mumbai," says Cotton.

Heading: Class paper - Indian Express
Content:
Vimla Devi took on the civic establishment to get public toilets in Trilokpuri running

When Vimla Devi saw the unhygienic conditions the residents of slum clusters in Trilok Puri were living in and how they had converted a nearby scrubland into a toilet, she decided to take action. "I could not tolerate how the civic authorities had turned a blind eye to the people in the clusters. The public conveniences were either totally rundown or were under lock and key," says the 55-year-old social worker.

The long struggle—which involved filing a series of RTI applications and writing letters to the civic establishment—to get clean and functional toilets for the residents of the slums finally yielded results in March 2007. Now there are two fully functional public toilets in the area and five more are being renovated. "When I visited the slums in 2006 with a friend working for a Delhi-based NGO, I was shocked. There was filth all over the place, garbage was strewn around and the toilets were non-functional. The residents did not even know that government sweepers were supposed to clean up the area. Something had to be done to bring some dignity back into the lives of the slum-dwellers," argues Devi.

Clueless how to bring about change, she approached the Centre For Advocacy Research (CFAR) for help and was able to rally support for the cause. Soon she gathered women living in the cluster to form the Mahila Pragati Manch, a platform to fight for better amenities in their area. "I figured that single-handedly I would stand a lesser chance of bringing in change. So I got support from women to face the civic bodies," she explains.

In 2006, she submitted an application to the government under the RTI Act against the closure of the toilets and unclean surroundings. The RTI threw up some startling revelations. "It said that the toilets were alright and functional. But when we approached the MCD, they turned a deaf ear to us. So I approached CFAR again," she says.

Armed with a small video recorder, Devi shot a four-minute film capturing the condition of the toilets and the surroundings. "When the film was shown to the Lt Governor of Delhi, he issued orders for action to be taken at the earliest. But it was not until the intervention of the Chief Minister in March 2007 that repair work began in earnest," she says. Now the people in the slums use the toilets and do not have to run to the scrubland.

Rambai, who has lived in the area for 12 years, is grateful. "It is because of Didi that I have become aware of my rights. She showed us how to fight for our rights," says Rambai.

Devi is not resting on her achievement. She is now trying to get ration cards issued to the residents of the slums. Ask Devi why she helps strangers and she says, "It is satisfying to be able to help someone in need. My mother taught me this lesson early in childhood."

Heading: Pulotsav kicks off; Vijaya Mehta awarded Pu La Smruti Sanman - Indian Express
Content:
It's time for the weekly meeting and at least 18 of the 25 members constituting an editorial team have assembled to brainstorm on topics, stories, visuals and design for the next issue of their journal. Rijuta Lamba, the editor, believes that the focus of the next issue should be disability. After all, there's very little information available on the various types of disabilities and people usually associate it solely with physical handicap and autism, she argues with her colleagues.

Nothing extraordinary about this editorial meeting but for the fact that all the 'editors', 'reporters' and 'visualisers' are students of class IX and XI.

They are working on The Yamuna, a magazine—as one of them describes it—for the children and by the children. What's noteworthy is the fact that the topics that this quarterly magazine focuses on are not really regular kids stuff. From food security to the role of the media, these young adults take serious views on issues that concern society and take out a journal that's packed with new thoughts and new ideas.

The next issue is due in January, but with their examination scheduled for December, there's not much time left.

Started in 2003, The Yamuna is part of a media literacy project started by the Gandhi Smriti. The aim is to develop a critical understanding of the media among children and young adults. Every year, one student from class XI is chosen to become the editor. Though Delhi contributes the maximum number of student-journalists working on the magazine, there are child-reporters in far flung areas of the country—from Guwahati in Assam to Koraput in Orissa to Belgaum in Karnataka to Solan in Himachal Pradesh— who contribute stories for the journal. At times, outstation reporters write in their mother tongue and the editorial team has to get it translated into English. But the real challenge, as Rijuta puts it, is to coordinate online with reporters based at Mexico City and Kathmandu who come up with news and views from their parts of the world.

While for class IX student Isha, the magazine is an opportunity to write, for Pearl it is an opportunity to interact with people from diverse background. If Himanshi associates the thrill of meeting celebrities like Mike Pandey with the magazine, for Akhilesh, it provides a platform to contribute to society—even if it's in small measure, he says.

Every working Saturday, the group meets to discuss the nitty-gritty as well as to allot duties and assignments. Every aspect, from the way a particular story should be written to illustrations or photographs accompanying it, from the masthead to the standalone graphics, are thrashed out. As Keshava puts it, "The sheer exposure that The Yamuna has provided all of us is phenomenal." Adds Seema, "Periodic interactions with children from Mexico City and Kathmandu as well as from the tribal belt of the country have opened a new world for me."

Of course, some of them want to become journalists when they grow up, but for now they are happy with their own newspaper and confident that their views on the media and other burning issues can be the first step towards change.

Heading: Residents protest tree felling in Aga Khan palace premises - Indian Express
Content:
Veteran Marathi writer V D Karandikar on Saturday inaugurated the sixth Pulotsav at Yashwantrao Chavan Auditorium by lighting the traditional lamp. "Pu La was a multifaceted personality. Filled with various events like short films, plays, literature and music, Pulotsav is a great cultural initiative. I congratulate the organisers and wish them all the success," Karandikar said.

Pulotsav, in memory of late P L Deshpande has kicked off on his birthday, this year.

Later in the event, senior theatre personality Vijaya Mehta was awarded Pu La Smruti Sanman, which consists of a memento and Rs 1,00,000 by Karandikar.

"I had the opportunity to observe Pu La's personality very closely. He taught me various aspects of theatre. One of the best lessons I have learnt from him was that a play is nothing but sharing one's happiness with the audience. He left a great impact on me. Today, receiving an award named after him is a great feeling. I accept this award with great pleasure," said an emotional Vijaya Mehta, receiving the award.

Narendra Jadhav, Vice Chancellor of University of Pune, who was present at the event said, "The number of cultural programmes taking place in the city is much more compared to that in other cities. I am hopeful that along with Pulotsav, a number of other art-related activities will also find a platform here."

Author Meena Prabhu was the chief guest for the function. Also present on the occasion were Shashank Paranjpe, managing director, Paranjape schemes, Virendra Chitrao, organiser, Sarang Lagoo and Neena Kulkarni, actress.

As part of the 13-day festival, a number of events like Tribute to Rohini Bhate, screening of films on Pandit Bhimsen Joshi and interaction with Radio Jockeys will take place at various locations in the city. On November 18, the first Pulotsav Krutadnyata Sanman will be presented to Dr Prakash Amte and Dr Manda Amte. Also, Pulotsav Jeevan Gaurav Sanman will be presented to veteran actor Sulochana. After Pune, the festival will be conducted throughout the state.

Heading: City to get hanging garden near Sarasbaug - Indian Express
Content:
'Most of the trees are over hundred years old and rare'

Residents living in the neighborhood of the historical Aga Khan Palace are up in arms against a private builder, who has allegedly been cutting down trees for land development purposes. The agitated residents have approached the commissioner of Pune Municipal Corporation demanding to stop the felling of trees.

They have submitted a memorandum of demands to the commissioner, in which they say, "Most of the trees are over hundred years old. But the builder is trying to reap selfish benefits by by cutting them."

"The Aga Khan compound has large number of huge rare trees, which keep the area around, one of the busiest localities in the city, greener. Cutting down the huge and rare trees in large numbers must not be permitted under any circumstances to serve purely private interests of the builders," the memorandum says.

Heading: Yet another fake letter with CM’s signature - Indian Express
Content:
The Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) will construct a hanging garden around the Adambaug mosque at Sadashiv Peth near Sarasbaug. The decision was taken late on Friday, after the civic body held discussions with the members of the Nagori Muslim Misgar Jamat Trust. The issue was long pending and had witnessed a lot of controversy.

The hanging garden is to be constructed on the Adambaug land excluding the particular mosque location.

The PMC has started laying a barbed wire fence around the site from Saturday to protect the land site. The decision was taken after trust members' approval for the project, after the meetings.

Heading: Flouting rule not a ‘berth’ right - Indian Express
Content:
The Shivajinagar police have registered a complaint against an unknown person on Saturday in connection with a fake letter bearing chief minister Vilasrao Deshmukh's signature, which was sent to the PMC.

The incident comes barely days after another person was produced in the court for having sent a fake letter to the commissioner's office accusing two people of having links with the SIMI and slain gangster Robert Salve.

The police had recovered many other fake letters and government files from his residence. Seals, stamps and letterheads of various state departments were also found.

In the letter, which carried a forged signature of the chief minister and sent to the PMC, the person had claimed that there was mismanagement in the conduct of the examination for the electricity department class four candidates in the PMC.

The letter, which called for stopping the recruitment process was delivered on august 14. Later, it was found that the letter was a fake one.

It stated that the Maharashtra State Nagar Vikas Mantralaya had sent the letter and called for immediate action.

PMC vice president, Yeshwant Khaire filed a complaint at Shivajinagar police station.

The police are trying to find out whether Sunil Pawar, who had recently been arrested for sending a fake letter, was behind this one too.

Heading: In Pune, Dalai Lama stresses on Gandhian values - Indian Express
Content:
Errant sleeper coach buses breaking rules to be reined in

The Regional Transport Office and the traffic police today decided to take action against errant owners of sleeper coach buses that often carry more passengers than provided for, thus flouting safety norms. Sleeper coaches have been found to often pack in more than one person for each berth.

In a meeting today, the RTO and the traffic police took note of all norms flouted by sleeper coach buses.

"The Regional Transport Office has assured us that they would provide us with sufficient manpower to crack down on owners of sleeper buses who flout norms," said DCP, traffic police, Manoj Patil.

He said there had been three accidents involving sleeper coaches in the state in the recent weeks, where the buses had been carrying excess passengers and flouting other norms as well. "We have taken action against one bus recently," said Patil.

The authorities were spurred into action because of a complaint made to the chief minister's office on October 3, 2008, which was passed down to various transport departments, including the RTO this week.

The complainant narrated his own experience and said: "In a 20-seater sleeper bus, there were approximately 54 travellers. Berths had two passengers and in one case, three people were made to share one berth; because of the quarrel that ensued with the driver, there was an accident."

A member of the "Sarthak Sanghatana" had written the letter. The complainant also pointed out that the government was losing revenue for every extra passenger thus ferried illegally.

According to "the Maharastra Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989", berths in sleeper buses are required to have the following standards in size: 1.75 metre in length, width not less than 0.76 metre and not more than 0.9 metre — which means that not more than one person can be given one berth. It also makes air-conditioning compulsory. "Public service vehicle shall be equipped with air-conditioning unit of adequate cooling capacity," the rules say.

"It is true that each berth should have only one passenger. Some travellers flout norms and give us a bad name," said Pratap Aidasani, Royal Travels, a sleeper bus operator. He said often passengers did not pay for the air-conditioning and therefore owners switch off the AC. There are around 100-150 sleeper buses operating from the city. Buses from Pune ply to four neighbouring states: Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Goa. They also carry passengers within the state.

Heading: Govt officials directed to take immediate action against erring subordinates - Indian Express
Content:
"India and Tibet share a teacher-disciple relationship, and if a disciple suffers, the teacher is responsible for it," observed Dalai Lama, Tibetan leader.

The Dalai Lama was in the city on Saturday to inaugurate the Gita Mandir at Sadhu Vaswani Mission. He also attended the concluding day of the 42nd Sarvodaya Samaj Sammelan.

Speaking at the Mission's function, he spoke about human relations to politics. The spiritual leader said that Tibet changed into a civilised society only when India's message of love reached there. "Teachings of Buddha gave direction to the life of Tibetans. So, even if China has substantial control over our land, the people there look up to India for support and love," he said.

He urged that while supporting the cause of Tibet's liberation, ecological, culural and humanitarian grounds should be given more importance than politics. Stressing on a friendly India, China relationship, he said, "Genuine friendship between India and China will not only make the world a safer place but also help in Tibet liberation."

"People have had a century of bloodshed and killing and now they have realised the importance of peace. World peace will be achieved only when one practices inner peace."

The disarmament may also mean to practice forgiveness and spiritual reconciliation. "Dialogue can help us avoid many conflicts at home and also beyond borders," he said.

While felicitating the Dalai Lama on the occasion, J P Vaswani said, "The Dalai Lama is humble yet strong enough to stand against a mighty nation like China."

At the Sarvodaya Samaj Sammelan, the Dalai Lama highlighted India's long history of non violence and tolerance. "India should strive to spread these values throughout the world," he said.

The Dalai Lama spoke about his two-point programme that should be emphasised upon — the first one is Ahimsa and the second one is promotion of religious harmony. He said, "It is gladdening to see that even after so many years, Gandhiji's values, ideology and principles are deep rooted in the Indian way of life. It is nice to see that in India people continue to practice non-violence despite many hardships and struggles."

The three-day long Sammelan had several Gandhian followers from India and around the world as speakers.

Heading: Sanstha asked to return money to five members - Indian Express
Content:
The state government has recently issued a regulation directing government officials to take immediate disciplinary action against subordinate officials, if proofs of corruption and irregularities found under Right to Information Act (RTI) or other sources. Besides, the state government has also directed them to make use of the appropriate computerised system to keep a check on the timely attendance of the employees.

These directions are fallout of a meeting that Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh had with social crusader Anna Hazare on August 13. The regulation was issued on November 1.

The state government directions mention that if a government official is found to be deliberately evading his duties, a disciplinary action against him should immediately be initiated. The regulation also directs to appoint a complaint redressal system in every district against such officials, which will work as watchdogs and follow up the issue till action is taken against the erring officials.

If the senior official fails to or deliberately evades immediate disciplinary action against erring subordinates, then the district level watchdogs could take disciplinary action against the senior officials, the regulation says.

Heading: Labourers turn gold diggers, caught - Indian Express
Content:
The consumer court has passed a ruling in favour of five members of the Rajyog Gramin Bigar Sheti Shahakari Pathsanstha Maryadit, where in they will be paid the entire amount they had deposited with the Sanstha six years ago.

The five members of the Pathsanstha had deposited amounts varying from Rs 4,800 up to Rs 20,000 at 14 per cent interest rate in 2002. The principal amount, along with the interest, was due to the members after a period of one year. However, even after one year, in 2003, the Sanstha refused to pay the amount to the members.

The five members — Asha Tanawade, Sandeep Dhume, Abashaeb Kale, Suresh Tanawade and Chandrakant Jadhav — moved the consumer court and filed a complaint against the Pathsanstha.

Prosecution lawyer Kiran Ghone said, "The five people had filed the complaint in 2006. After the court heard both the sides, judge P K Gaikwad has passed a decision in their favour. The Sanstha will now have to pay not only the amount deposited by the members but also the interest on it at the rate of 14 per cent per annum right from 2002 to 2008."

Heading: Master of ceremonies - Indian Express
Content:
Pot of gold: ancient coins unearthed from pool site

The site for a swimming pool at a PMC-run school has thrown up a treasure — a copper vessel full of ancient gold coins.

Labourers found the coins worth around Rs 42 lakh (cost of the gold) while they were digging the earth for the construction of a swimming pool at N V Gadgil School run by Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) in Shaniwar Peth.

The labours sold about half the coins to a Khadki-based jeweller and were planning to flee with the rest when, acting on a tip off, the crime branch of Pune police nabbed them as well as the jeweller and recovered 847 gold coins weighing around 3.2 kg on Friday. The coins made of 24-carat gold are believed to be about 500 years old.

The police have arrested three labourers identified as Shivappa Husnappa Gadekar (40) of Tingre Nagar in Vishrantwadi, Mallesh Parashram Nadvinkari (25) from Karnataka and Bhimsha Pitappa Bansode (40) from Solapur and the jeweller Surajbhan Agarwal under sections of Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958.

Deputy Commissioner of Police (crime) Anil Kumbhare said, "Most of the coins carry the mark of a saint, referred to as protector of Venice in Italy on one side and of infant Jesus on the other. These are Roman coins from the medieval period. The remaining coins are the "asharfis" or "mohurs" having Urdu and Persian inscriptions and were in use during Akbar's regime in the 15 th century."

Kumbhare said the labourers found the coins on Thursday while digging. "Constable Bapusaheb Jadhav of the Anti Dacoity Squad (ADS) obtained this information from his sources. Following the inputs, a team led by inspector Ram Pathare of ADS nabbed the three labourers. From the labourers, the police recovered 425 coins weighing 1.5 kg worth around Rs 20 lakh," he said. "Interrogations revealed they had sold more coins to Shri Ganesh Jewellers in Khadki. So the police nabbed the jeweller and seized 422 coins weighing 1.65 kg worth Rs 22 lakh from him," he added.

The police said the labourers did not even inform their superiors at the construction site and had plans to escape with the coins. The jeweller was arrested for not informing the police when the labourers approached him to sell the coins.

ACP Sangramsinh Nishandar said Archeological Survey of India (ASI) authorities will be studying the coins. They would be handing over the coins to the ASI after obtaining the permission from the court.

Heading: Melting Pots - Indian Express
Content:
As the wedding season starts after Kartik Purnima, pundits in the city will be having the busiest schedules

Lavish reception, exuberant theme parties, bachelors' night, sangeet sandhya, scrumptious food, vibrant dressing and jewelry – all you can picture with this is the big Indian wedding bash. But while weddings may change in terms of magnitude and grandeur, the one aspect that has remained unaltered over the years is the presence and importance of the pundit, the one who solemnises the knot of love.

Be it the long-standing tradition of Hindu weddings or the fast-track marriages in a court, solemnising the conjugal life of a couple has been a ritual obeyed for ages in all castes and communities. Shilpa and Satish Jain, who married in the court reveal, "After the registration, a traditional marriage ceremony was also held at home which was formalised by the pundit." Adding to this 31-year-old pandit Milind Sant, who has solemnised around 60 marriages, says, "Even today many people still prefer the traditional style wedding. Solemnising marriages has been our job always and after Kartik purnima, the wedding season will start and then we would be having very busy schedules."

The Hindu wedding muhurats, which are seasonal and occuring mainly between October and May will see more traditional style wedding this year as compared to the previous year, adds Sant, who has received training by his guru for the work he does.

"Keeping in mind the muhurat system most of the wedding ceremonies are being held in the months of October, November and December this year. It is the time when most of the working professionals have their vacations too," says Pandit Pradeep Joshi who has solemnised more than a hundred marriages. He feels it's important to follow the muhurats to avoid any risks in married life.

"Keeping in mind the rush, we would have to work overtime in this season and may a time end up conducting more than three marriages in a day," says Sant. Suneeta Gadge, a trained priest under Jnana Prabodhini, who has been practising since the last 17 years says she also has a hugely busy schedule this month. "Muhurat for marriages start after Tulsi vivaah, each community has different timings, like the Gujaratis have their muhurats at dawn and Maharashtrians prefer afternoon. Hence a priest can solemnise two such weddings on the same day. We have our group of pundits also, so there is no issue even if two weddings are scheduled in the same muhurat. Also, these days 70 per cent of marriage halls have personalised priests," says pundit Tejas Lakshman Saptarishiage who is practicing since the last nine years. While the next two months will see the pundits of the city in high demand as they rush from one place to another to soleminse ceremonies that cannot be completed without their presence, what do they do once the situaion eases? Saptarishiage provides an answer. "During off-season when there are no marriages then I get into astrology and vastushastra," he says.

Heading: ‘Abs’-olutely hot - Indian Express
Content:
Pardesi Felicitated
Advocate Pratap Pardesi and his colleges renovated the Lakshmibai Dutta Mandir, on Lakshmi road, which is one of the oldest temples of Pune. In a Recent function organised by the trustees of the temple, advocate Pratap Pardesi was felicitated at the hands of Tatyasaheb Godse, President, Sarvajanic Ganesh Trust on been elected as President of Smt. Lakshmibai Dutta Mandir Trust. The state information commissioner Vijay Kuwadekar was also present as the chief guest of the function.

Dhamma Chakra Pravartan
Dalit Panther of India celebrated Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din recently. Founder president of Dalit Panther of India, Bapusaheb Bhosale presented Rajratna Buddha Vihar on Tadiwala road with an idol of lord Gautam Buddha. On the same occasion set of books on Gautam Buddha and Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar were handed over to Nagsen library in Camp. Students are requested to make use of this library.

Divine art
The Shree Muthappan Charitable Foundation is organising Theyyam, an art form performed generally in north Kerala at Kalewadi in Pimpri on November 9. The dance form will see the dancer dressed in traditional attire. According to the organisers, the dance performers will perform on Lord Muthappan, an incarnation of Lord Shiva in a tribal form. Muthappan is the presiding deity of Parassini Madappura and Kunnathurpadi in Kannur district in Kerala. The dance performance will take off at 9 am onwards at the Jyotiba Mangal Karyalay.

Sweet Takes
Every year the Mahalakshmi temple near Sarasbaug celebrates Annakot when Goddess Mahalakshmi is offered 56 different sweets. This year 500 children from the Santulan Pashan school, which caters to children of stone mine workers, were invited for the celebration on November 3. The trustees of the temple also provided these children with school stationary of daily use.

Abhishek ceremony
Shree Akhil Bharatiya Tirth Prabhavak Adhar Abhishek Anusthan Samitee is organising 18 Abhishek Ceremony in three parts for more than 100-year-old Jain temples. In Maharashtra, this ceremony will be held on Sunday, November 23. The ceremony shall be performed on about one-lakh idols of 10,000 Jain temples in three parts, throughout India. According to the principles of Jainism, the 18 Abhishek Ceremony removes impurity and brings serenity, tranquility and piousness. The complete expenses for the ceremony will be borne by an anonymous donor. Around 10,000 Jain youths are being trained to perform this pooja ceremony. It will be preformed as per the specific timings provided in the Jain religion for this purpose.

Skandshashti festival celebrated
Skandshashti festival was celebrated at the Shanmukhnanda Sabha, which is 54 years old.
All religious rituals like pooja, abhishek and chanting of Subramania Sahasranama was performed at the Karthikswami temple at Parvati hill. The event concluded with Deeparadhana to Lord Karthikswami. Priest VS Natraj Sastrigal performed the religious rituals at the temple. The temple trustees coordinated the program.

Kojagiri celebration held
On account of Kojagiri Poornima, Bhorde Ali took out a huge procession. Founder president of Dalit Panther of India, Bapusaheb Bhosale inaugurated the procession and preformed an aarti. The procession was accompanied by traditional music band.

Heading: The stage is her world - Indian Express
Content:
Just a couple of weeks back Aamir's eight-pack abs made a blaring entry to the fitness world when Ghajini's promos hit the screen. As the first actor in Bollywood to flaunt eight-pack abs walked the screen exuding incredible sex appeal, Shah Rukh's OSO's six-pack abs just about faded into oblivion. As fitness trainers in the city grapple with the flood of demands from fitness freaks for the all-new eight-pack abs, you know Bollywood has struck again.

Walk into a fitness centre in the city and you'll find special programmes on for eight-pack abs while muscle maniacs sweat it out with extra crunches, sit ups and leg lifts to get that perfectly toned and shaped torso.

Twenty-four year-old, software developer, Samir Madhani who aims to appear for Gladrags mega model hunt next year increased the hours for his workout the moment promos of Aamir Khan's recent film, Ghajini hit the screen. Madhani who works out on a regular basis at More Effective Health Club at Hadapsar did not want to lag behind in the race. "Once the film is released, it will be eight-packs which people will be looking for in a model and not six," says Madhik.

While Madhani works out to develop his eight packs, Nitin More his fitness trainer puts his act together to add the extra inputs to the fitness programme. "There is not much difference between developing six and eight-pack abs. In fact it's the same way as for a six-pack-just more intensive. But what can you do to get on with the process is making sure that you keep the momentum going and arrive at your goal without becoming too side tracked. Also eight-packs largely depend on body structure. So we have decided to design a programme which apart from the exercises will also clear the myths attached to developing abs," says More. According to More the height and the width of the abdominal region decides whether one can develop eight-pack abs or not. "Not everyone can develop eight-pack abs. It largely depends on the body structure," asserts More

Rekha Khandelwal, Abs fitness centre, ICC Towers that too has clients asking for developing eight-pack abs concurs with More on who can reach that state of fitness. "Abs are small muscles in your body. Toning them is all about reducing fat and developing muscles. Once you reduce fat, it will be visible on its own. But as far as eight-pack abs is concerned, it's all about an individual's body structure. It's all one muscle; it just has tendons running across it. The packs depend on how thick the tendon is and the length of the muscle itself. Those with a short tendon will probably be able to get an eight pack." So do you qualify? If so, go get it!

Heading: Split into two at bridge function - Indian Express
Content:
Theatre personality Vijaya Mehta says she has no regrets about not having an entity independent of theatre

Rangakarmi, bai, theatrical doyen- the world might have added a list of adjectives to her name but she explains herself in one simple line- I am a sponge. In an open interaction with actress and student Neena Kulkarni and Ambarish Mishra, senior director, actor and theatre personality Vijaya Mehta unveiled her theatrical journey at the sixth Pulotsav at Yashwantrao Chavan Auditorium.

"I call myself a sponge because I kept my senses open in order to learn more. I did not keep knocking for an opportunity but when the doors opened, I did not say no to the opportunities either. When I recollect the various phases of my life, I like myself as Vijaya Jaywant the most because as a young, energetic girl, I had the urge to take the best from everyone around me. I was thankfully surrounded by connoisseurs like Ebrahim Alkazi, Adi Marzban, Plitz Dinovit and so on and I learnt the best from them all," says Mehta.

While the opinions of these personalities helped her in developing an approach, what sets Mehta apart is the independent philosophy that she preached through her organisation Rangayan and other theatrical ventures. In Mehta's own words, "A good theatre personality can be judged by three aspects. He or she should not be a speaker but a teller, not a hearer but a listener and lastly not a viewer but a watcher. Talking about drama, what is important according to me is the concept and theme of the play and not the script. Plays based on scripts are more like clothes tailormade to suit the audiences' needs. I tried to do a couple of them and realised that it is not my style of working."

With a number of commercial, theme-based plays like Barister, Purush, Hameedabaichi kothadi, Wada Chirebandi and multi lingual plays like Shakuntal, Nagmandal and Mudra Rakshas to her credit, Mehta adds, "Theatre does not have a language. You won't believe but I got a better understanding of Sanskrit theatre in Germany." Explaining theatre with an example Mehta elaborates, "Theatre is like rangoli. It is for the moment. Drama takes shape through an amalgamation of performers and audience. And the way a rangoli is wiped after the auspicious day, drama also is because what comes out the next day is a different amalgamation again."

Known for creating names in the film industry like Neena Gupta, Vikram Gokhale, Nana Patekar and so on , Mehta's entry into cinema compared to her theatrical stint was quite late. She explains, "I entered late because I realised it quite late after watching films of people like Shyam Benegal that portrayal of similar expressions is possible through films as a medium as well."

Commenting on the current scenario in Marathi theatre Mehta feels, "The most important aspect in theatre is dedication. Theatre is not possible without time and unfortunately no one has time today. I must say that there is potential even today. Give me artistes and time and I will bring back the lost glory." On a concluding note she says, "Today, when I look at the years gone by, I feel that other than theatre, I do not have an independent existence. There are good memories and bad memories but thankfully the ones that surround me and keep me going are the ones that are good."

Heading: Hit by failure, engineering student commits suicide - Indian Express
Content:
Political play, damage control at foundation ceremony

It was intended to be one function. But the cornerstone-laying ceremony for the new Holkar Bridge was virtually split into two events on Saturday, one led by Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) and the second conducted by the Congress.

In the first half, Mayor Rajlaxmi Bhosale of the NCP wound up the function and hurriedly left the spot, apparently to avoid meeting Congress MP Suresh Kalmadi, who reached the venue about half-an-hour late after his arrival from Delhi.

The Congress later carried on with its own agenda, amounting to starting a function that had almost ended, again.

The function was organised by the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) to mark the beginning of the construction of the two new add-on bridges parallel to the existing Holkar Bridge.

The event was scheduled to take place at 10.30 am in the presence of district Guardian Minister Ajit Pawar and Suresh Kalmadi. As Pawar did not turn up, the mayor presided over the function. She, however, opted not to wait for Kalmadi and disappeared after a 20-minute event.

Despite all this, Kalmadi seemed in no mood for a confrontation with NCP and refrained from using any bitter words on the turn of events. "One should ignore and forget such trifles and concentrate on work with a sportsman spirit. The city's progress is more important. The mayor must have left due to some other commitments," he said, adding, "The development of the city should be given priority over such issues and hence the Congress has decided to co-operate with the mayor."

In the morning, at the NCP function before Kalmadi's arrival, defence officials Lt Gen Noble Thamburaj, General Officer Commanding-in-chief, Southern Command, and Brigadier Sanjeev Talwar, commandant Bombay Engineering Group were felicitated. Congress MLA Chandrakant Chhajed was present.

This was followed by a short speech by the mayor. Immediately afterwards she is believed to have given instructions that the function should be wound up and the vote of thanks given. Interestingly, Thamburaj got a chance to speak only after the vote of thanks.

To add to the confusion, after Thamburaj's speech, the defence personnel started removing the tents, presuming the function was over. But then, Congress corporator Ulhas Bagul announced that Kalmadi was on his way. By then, the mayor, NCP corporators and the civic as well as defence officials had left.

On his arrival, Kalmadi gave his speech and was then led up to the cornerstone by Congress workers. Mid-way, the MP realised that it had already been inaugurated and he turned back.

Later, interacting with the media, Kalmadi tried to make light of the episode. "The mayor must have left early to attend some other event. I came to Pune especially for this event despite my commitments in Delhi. Many people from Khadki Cantonment Board were disgruntled as they were not invited, but I asked them to overlook such issues and strive for developmental work," he said.

He added that he was doing all this for Pune's sake and not for the Lok Sabha elections. "I do not wish to spoil the feel-good atmosphere set after the Commonwealth Youth Games (CYG)," he added.

Before this event, the mayor also inaugurated Gurunam Academy, a hostel facility being jointly raised by PMC at BEG for children of jawans who attained martyrdom during war. As per the PMC plans, the add-on bridges to the historic Holkar Bridge will be completed by 2010 at a cost of Rs 61 crore. These bridges will help ease traffic snarls commuters put up with at present.
